categories.label: EPC/Single-Point Responsibility Risk Transfer
categories.memo: Covers how EPC and design-build models consolidate design, procurement, and construction responsibility into a single entity, shifting risk away from owners/developers.

codes.label: Consolidation of design-procurement-construction responsibility
codes.description: EPC/DB general contractor assumes near-total responsibility for design, procurement, and construction, providing owners a single point of responsibility and shifting most project risk to the contractor.

codes.label: Design risk within EPC prefabrication
codes.description: Design risk in EPC prefabricated projects is concentrated in insufficiently in-depth design and poor coordination between design and other disciplines/stages.

codes.label: Integrated design-procurement coordination
codes.description: EPC enables procurement to be integrated with design, as material/component needs are determined during design, allowing joint decision-making by purchasers, designers, and engineers.

codes.label: Construction-stage risk dominance
codes.description: Construction risk, particularly stability of temporary support systems for precast components, is identified as the largest risk category in EPC prefabricated projects, exceeding design, procurement, and management risk.

codes.label: Procurement quality and supplier risk
codes.description: Quality defects and transportation damage of precast components are major procurement-stage risks requiring supplier vetting and incentive systems under EPC.

codes.label: Fixed-price economic risk exposure
codes.description: EPC's typically fixed-price structure concentrates economic risk (payment delays, rising material costs) on the contractor, a significant contractual concern.

codes.label: Management/coordination risk in EPC
codes.description: Insufficient project management experience and poor inter-unit communication are recurring management risks, requiring integrated supply chain management capability beyond simple superposition of functions.

codes.label: Regulatory/policy environment effects on risk
codes.description: Maturity of regional prefabrication policy and regulation affects the level of policy-related risk borne by EPC project parties.

codes.label: EPC-prefabrication research/practice gap
codes.description: Scarcity of research and standardized contractual practice specifically addressing prefabrication risk within EPC delivery represents an ongoing knowledge gap.

codes.label: Fast-tracking and constructability feedback under DB
codes.description: DB allows construction to begin before design completion and enables contractor constructability input, reducing later change orders and delays.

codes.label: Owner control trade-offs under DB risk transfer
codes.description: DB delivery carries risks/disadvantages for owners including reduced control, higher cost of owner-requested changes, and potential higher overall cost due to risk transfer to the contractor.

categories.label: Risk Allocation Frameworks in Bundled Project Delivery
categories.memo: Addresses the unique risk allocation and dependency issues that arise when multiple projects are bundled under a single contract, comparing DBB and DB responses.

codes.label: Mutual dependence risk in bundled DBB contracts
codes.description: Bundling projects under DBB creates a risk of mutual dependence, where an issue at one project location can delay or block the entire bundled contract from being advertised.

codes.label: DB mitigation of bundled dependency risk
codes.description: Under DB, the design-builder can assume full responsibility for permits, utilities, and ROW negotiations across all bundled sites, mitigating the dependency risk inherent in DBB bundling.

codes.label: Complex scheduling and third-party coordination risk
codes.description: Bundled contracts require managing complex construction sequencing, third-party coordination (utilities, ROW, permits, railroads), and traffic management across multiple locations under one aggressive schedule.

codes.label: Financing and contract-size risk in bundling
codes.description: Larger bundled contract size increases funding/financing considerations and risk exposure for owner agencies compared to single-project contracts.

codes.label: Applicability gap of PDM selection tools to bundled contracts
codes.description: Existing PDM selection frameworks were developed for single, non-bundled projects and do not directly address the distinct risk profile of bundled contracts.

categories.label: IPD Contractual Risk-Sharing Mechanisms
categories.memo: Focuses on how IPD and relational contract structures formalize shared risk/reward, liability limitation, incentive compensation, and dispute resolution as explicit contractual provisions.

codes.label: Multiparty shared risk/reward structure
codes.description: IPD is defined by multiparty agreements, shared risk and reward, and early involvement of all parties, distinguishing its risk allocation from conventional delivery methods.

codes.label: Proactive vs reactive risk management
codes.description: Regardless of delivery method, the underlying project risk is the same; IPD arrangements aim to manage risk proactively rather than reactively through contractual structure.

codes.label: Liability allocation clarity and dispute causation
codes.description: Ambiguous or unclear allocation of liabilities among contracting parties is a leading cause of disputes, underscoring the need for precise contractual liability clauses.

codes.label: Suspension and termination rights ambiguity
codes.description: Ambiguity in contractual rights and obligations regarding suspension and termination under negotiated IPD agreements is a recurring source of dispute.

sub_codes.label: Termination discretion asymmetry between standard forms
sub_codes.description: Standard contract forms vary in the discretion given to owners to terminate, with some forms placing other parties at a disadvantage due to fewer restrictions on notice.

codes.label: Risk assessment technique specification in standard forms
codes.description: Standard contracts differ in whether they mandate explicit risk-scoring/assessment techniques or leave the approach to the parties' discretion.

codes.label: Financial incentive and risk pool mechanisms
codes.description: Risk pool plans and financial incentive programs are used to align contractor/design professional performance with cost and schedule targets under IPD contracts.

codes.label: Liability limitation and waiver provisions
codes.description: Standard forms differ in how they cap or waive liability for claims, affecting the risk exposure each party bears, e.g., limiting liability to risk pool share or savings.

codes.label: Insurance requirement specificity
codes.description: Standard forms differ in specificity of insurance requirements and whether an insurance consultant is mandatory, reflecting differing risk-transfer approaches.

codes.label: BIM/data protocol compliance as contractual obligation
codes.description: Formalized BIM and data-sharing protocols in IPD contracts create enforceable obligations, with non-compliance treated as breach and grounds for withholding payment.

codes.label: Structured dispute escalation and resolution
codes.description: IPD contracts typically require internal escalation and mediation before binding dispute resolution methods such as arbitration or litigation, and proactive contractual checklists can reduce ambiguity that leads to disputes.

codes.label: Implementation gaps in inexperienced IPD teams
codes.description: Parties without prior IPD experience may fail to fully customize or implement standard risk/incentive provisions, undermining intended risk-sharing effectiveness.

categories.label: Liability Frameworks for Digital Fabrication
categories.memo: Concerns structured allocation of liability across actors, conditions, and resources specific to digital fabrication/off-site processes, and how delivery model choice shapes needed contractual supplements.

codes.label: Design-fabrication information handoff liability
codes.description: Misalignment between upstream design information and downstream digital fabrication execution creates liability uncertainty requiring clear contractual understanding.

codes.label: Resource-based liability factors (management/BIM expertise)
codes.description: Management capability and BIM expertise are identified as the most critical resource-related liability factors for successful digital fabrication adoption.

codes.label: Actor-based liability concentration in general contractor
codes.description: The general contractor bears the greatest liability responsibility among project actors due to oversight of the overall construction process including digital fabrication.

codes.label: Condition-based liability: constructability and early involvement
codes.description: On-site constructability and early contractor involvement are key condition-type liability factors, linking design-for-constructability practices to reduced digital fabrication liability risk.

codes.label: Delivery-model-specific liability allocation for digital fabrication
codes.description: Different project delivery models (DBB, IPD, etc.) allocate digital fabrication liability differently, with DBB's fragmentation creating more liability challenges and IPD's shared-risk structure requiring fewer supplementary contract provisions.

codes.label: Contractual mechanisms to embed liability factors
codes.description: Liability factors can be incorporated via supplementary agreements (e.g., PCSA), BIM protocols, standard agreement clauses, or practices like concurrent engineering to formally allocate digital fabrication risk.

categories.label: Developer-Contractor Risk Sharing and Incentive Contracting for Prefabrication
categories.memo: Covers game-theoretic and economic modeling of risk/benefit sharing between developers, general contractors and suppliers, including subsidy pass-through, revenue-sharing, and environmental responsibility incentive mechanisms.

codes.label: Asymmetric bargaining power between developer and contractor
codes.description: Developers hold informational and decision-making advantages over general contractors, shaping how prefabrication risk and responsibility are contractually allocated.

codes.label: Contractor as bearer of economic and quality risk
codes.description: General contractors assume primary economic and engineering-quality risk for implementing prefabrication under terms set by developers.

codes.label: Subsidy pass-through via revenue-sharing contracts
codes.description: Contracts can be structured to pass government subsidies from developer to contractor via revenue-sharing mechanisms to incentivize higher prefabrication levels.

sub_codes.label: Limits of simple revenue-sharing contracts
sub_codes.description: A simple revenue-sharing contract, even optimized, fails to achieve genuine win-win coordination, favoring the contractor over the developer due to information asymmetry.

sub_codes.label: Combined fixed-payment plus revenue-sharing contracts
sub_codes.description: Combining a fixed transfer payment with variable revenue-sharing can achieve genuine Pareto-improving coordination between developer and contractor.

codes.label: Regulatory benchmark thresholds affecting contractual uptake
codes.description: Assembly rate benchmarks set as contractual/regulatory thresholds affect enterprise willingness to adopt higher prefabrication levels due to added cost burdens.

codes.label: Information asymmetry and double marginalization
codes.description: Developer's inability to accurately observe contractor cost information creates a double marginalization effect, a structural driver of contractual inefficiency in prefabrication delivery.

codes.label: Environmental responsibility allocation between contractor and supplier
codes.description: Prefabrication redistributes environmental responsibility from on-site contractors to off-site suppliers; policy mechanisms tend to drive contractor and supplier toward equal sharing of environmental responsibility, with the contractor as central regulatory liaison.

codes.label: Government incentive/penalty mechanisms shaping contractual behavior
codes.description: Subsidy and reward-penalty government mechanisms directly shape the economic relationship between contractor and supplier, though reward-penalty mechanisms achieve better environmental outcomes at the cost of reduced profitability for both parties, and subsidy/contract design must be co-developed.

codes.label: Need for formal green procurement/coordination contracts
codes.description: Absent contractual coordination, neither contractor nor supplier is incentivized to invest in environmental responsibility; formal instruments like green procurement contracts or shared ER targets are needed to align supply chain sustainability efforts.

categories.label: Design Freeze, Early Involvement and Supplier Risk in Modular/Prefabricated Delivery
categories.memo: Concerns how the timing of design commitment, degree of contractor/manufacturer involvement, and choice of delivery model affect risk allocation and cost outcomes in modular and prefabricated construction.

codes.label: Early design freeze requirement
codes.description: Modular construction requires an early design freeze due to extensive pre-engineering needed before manufacturing, shifting risk toward early-stage decision accuracy.

codes.label: Manufacturer/contractor role in design phase
codes.description: Assigning manufacturers or contractors a larger, more determining role during design improves design-production compatibility and reduces downstream risk.

codes.label: Client risk-aversion to single-supplier commitment
codes.description: Clients often resist committing to a single modular supplier as a risk-averse contractual measure, affecting delivery model and contract structure choices.

codes.label: Suitability of integrated delivery models for modular risk-sharing
codes.description: Traditional DBB poorly accommodates modular construction's need for design-construction overlap; more integrated models (ECI, D&B, Turnkey) better distribute risk and enable optimization.

codes.label: Product-based versus project-based contracting
codes.description: Modular construction lacks long-term product-based contractual arrangements (framework/serial tendering); a shift toward Product Delivery Models with fixed long-term partnerships and standard product contracts is proposed to better allocate risk.

codes.label: System architect risk concentration
codes.description: The party developing the modular system typically becomes the 'system architect' responsible for design rules, shifting risk and responsibility away from the client.

codes.label: Two-stage tendering to de-risk technical feasibility
codes.description: A Pre-Service Contract Arrangement (two-stage tender) allows technical feasibility validation of a modular solution before committing to a Design & Build contract, reducing risk prior to full commitment.

codes.label: Developer cognition as a driver of cost/design-change risk
codes.description: Developer attitude and understanding of prefabricated construction shapes project definition, design accuracy, and BIM use, ultimately affecting design changes and on-site cost risk.

codes.label: Design changes as hidden transaction cost risk
codes.description: Design changes are a primary source of hidden transaction costs for developers, damaging reputation and future cooperation willingness, reinforcing the case for contractual design-freeze provisions.

codes.label: Contractual terms to enforce design accuracy and standardization
codes.description: Detailed contract terms can be used by developers to encourage and restrict designers toward improved accuracy and standardization, allocating design-quality risk contractually.

codes.label: Transaction cost risk from new procurement/approval processes
codes.description: Prefabricated construction introduces new procurement, approval, monitoring and negotiation transaction costs distinct from conventional construction, often overlooked in contractual risk allocation.

codes.label: Reconfigured stakeholder responsibility due to off-site shift
codes.description: The shift of activities to off-site production environments changes the responsibilities and risk allocation among PC stakeholders compared to conventional in-situ construction, requiring reconsideration of contractual roles.
